---
title: "Expected errors in a strict ranking"
subtitle: "1.16 · after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.B and slides 21–22"
description: "Posterior expected wrong-direction counts among the n(n − 1)/2 statements of a strict ranking."
---

A strict ranking states a direction for every unordered pair of units. For $n$ units it therefore makes
$M = n(n-1)/2$ statements, represented by the cells of a triangle. A statement that $i$ exceeds $j$ is wrong with
posterior probability $1 - \pi_{ij}$, where $\pi_{ij}$ is the probability that $i$ has the larger true value. Summing
these error probabilities gives the posterior expected number of incorrect statements. In the examples, uncertain
comparisons are concentrated among nearby ranks, although two imprecise units can remain difficult to order even
when widely separated in the displayed ranking ([The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities](pairwise-matrix.qmd)).

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **97 firms.** Kline, Rose and Walters' (KRW) firms, ranked by posterior mean, make 4,656 claims; the posterior expected wrong count is 1,249, more than one in four. Ranked by estimate they expect 1,395 (the two orders disagree on 639
  pairs); KRW find the posterior-mean order close to their best strict ranking (Section V.E), but that is not a general
  rule. Here 35 claims sit above one half.
- **Top 10 by posterior mean.** 45 claims, 18.22 expected wrong. The scale table sets them beside the 17,014,861
  claims of a ranking of the case study's 5,834 California schools (elementary-type schools with at least 30 students
  counted).
- **Six sites.** 15 claims, .7194 expected wrong. The highest dot, C above D, is a claim between neighbours, wrong with
  probability .362.
- **League of 30.** 435 claims; 94.48 expected wrong, 102.2 by estimate (37 pairs differ). Only a simulation knows the
  true values: 88 claims are wrong against them in this draw, 80.69 on average.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
KRW's race card at λ = 1 is also a full ranking, in a slightly different order, so it expects 1,248 wrong claims where
the posterior-mean order expects 1,249 ([KRW's archived reward path](../cases/krw-lambda.qmd)). The expected count is a sum
of probabilities over all the claims, not a list of particular claims. The data describe KRW's correspondence
experiment, not any firm's current conduct. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit
doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version), noncommercial use only. Changes: race pair
probabilities as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw); firms ranked here by posterior mean, top-n blocks and
expected counts computed in this browser. No endorsement is implied. School count: California Department of
Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, via postrank 1.1.0
(pr_case_cde); CDE source conditions apply
([https://www.cde.ca.gov/re/di/cr/index.asp](https://www.cde.ca.gov/re/di/cr/index.asp){style="word-break: break-all"});
only the statewide count is shown (changes noted); no CDE endorsement is implied.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
library(postrank)
m <- pr_case_krw$input$summaries$means[, "race_signed"]
postrank_evaluate(rank(-m), pr_case_krw$input, weights = c(race_signed = 1, gender_signed = 0), tau = .2)$E["race_signed"]   # 1248.868
```
:::
